text: Everything you've built so far — the bit-flip code, the phase-flip code, the Shor code — is a special case of one general framework. This lesson names that framework and shows precisely how your existing examples fit into it.

A stabilizer code is defined by a set of commuting Pauli operators, the stabilizer generators, such that the encoded logical states are exactly the simultaneous plus-1 eigenstates of all of them. An n-qubit code encoding k logical qubits needs n minus k independent generators. Check this against what you know: the 3-qubit bit-flip code has n equals 3, k equals 1, so n minus k equals 2 generators — exactly the Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 you worked with directly in Lesson 10. You were already using the stabilizer formalism, just without the general vocabulary.

A Pauli error E is detected by a stabilizer S exactly when they anticommute. An X error on qubit 1 anticommutes with Z1Z2, because X and Z anticommute on the same qubit, but commutes with Z2Z3, because qubit 1 isn't involved in that operator at all — giving exactly the syndrome 1, 0 you traced directly in Lesson 10's table. This single rule is what generates every syndrome table you've already verified by hand.

Alongside the stabilizers, every code has logical operators — Pauli operators that commute with every stabilizer, so they never trigger a syndrome, but act non-trivially on the encoded logical qubit itself. For the bit-flip code, Z-logical equals Z1, and X-logical equals X1 X2 X3. The real value of this framework is that once you describe a code purely as 'which Pauli operators are the stabilizers,' you can analyze any new code with the same commutation rule, without re-deriving a syndrome table by brute-force simulation.

That's exactly how the Steane code's 6 stabilizer generators, next lesson, and the surface code's dozens of local stabilizers in Chapter 5, get designed and analyzed — by choosing commuting Pauli operators with the right structure, not by hand-simulating every possible error.
